learn.hook: Your cricket team's scores were 12, 15, 9 and 120. Was the team's 'typical' score really 39? Different averages tell different stories!
points: Mean = sum of all values ÷ number of values.
For a frequency table: mean = Σ(f × x) ÷ Σf, where x is each value and f its frequency.
Median: arrange the data in order. For an odd count it is the middle value; for an even count it is the mean of the two middle values.
Mode is the value that occurs most often.
One very large or very small value (an outlier) pulls the mean a lot but hardly changes the median.

example.q: Find the mean and median of 4, 9, 2, 7, 3, 11.

learn.reallife: News reports often give the median house price or median salary, because a few very rich people would push the mean up a lot.

items.text: To find the median, first arrange the data in ___
The value that occurs most often is the ___
Sum of values ÷ number of values gives the ___
One very large value changes the ___ much more than the median

quiz.q: Find the mean of 4, 8, 6, 10 and 7.
quiz.explain: Sum = 35 and there are 5 values, so the mean is 35 ÷ 5 = 7.
quiz.mistake: Gives the sum without dividing, or picks the middle value of the unsorted list

quiz.q: Find the median of 3, 9, 1, 7, 6.
quiz.explain: In order: 1, 3, 6, 7, 9. The middle (3rd) value is 6.
quiz.mistake: Takes the middle of the unsorted list (1) without arranging the data first

quiz.q: Find the median of 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12.
quiz.explain: There are 6 values, so the median is the mean of the 3rd and 4th: (6 + 8) ÷ 2 = 7.
steps: Data in order: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12 (6 values, an even count).
Median = mean of the 3rd and 4th values = (6 + 8) ÷ 2
quiz.mistake: Picks one of the two middle values instead of their mean

quiz.q: Riya scored 72, 85, 90 and 78 in four tests. What must she score in the fifth test to make her mean exactly 80?
quiz.explain: For a mean of 80 over 5 tests she needs a total of 400. So far she has 325, so she needs 75.
quiz.mistake: Assumes she needs the target mean itself (80) in the last test

quiz.q: What is the mode of 2, 3, 3, 5, 7, 3, 5?
quiz.explain: 3 occurs three times, more than any other value.
steps: Count each value: 2 once, 3 three times, 5 twice, 7 once.
quiz.mistake: Finds the mean (4) instead of the most frequent value

quiz.q: In a class survey, 4 students have 1 pet, 3 have 2 pets and 3 have 3 pets. What is the mean number of pets?
quiz.mistake: Just averages the values 1, 2, 3 and ignores the frequencies, getting 2

quiz.q: Monthly pocket money of five friends: ₹200, ₹220, ₹250, ₹230 and ₹2000. Which average best shows what is typical?
options: The mean, because it uses every value
The median, because the mean is pulled up by one very large value
quiz.explain: The mean is ₹580, which is more than four of the five friends get. The median ₹230 is much more typical.
steps: Answer: The median, because the mean is pulled up by one very large value
quiz.mistake: Always trusts the mean, even when there is an outlier

quiz.q: The mean of 10 numbers is 15. Later it is found that 24 was wrongly copied as 42. What is the correct mean?
quiz.explain: The wrong total is 150. The correct total is 150 − 42 + 24 = 132, so the correct mean is 13.2.
quiz.mistake: Adds the difference of 18 instead of subtracting it, getting 16.8

teach.ask: Gappu has the numbers 5, 1, 9, 3, 7: "How do I find the mean and the median? Aren't they the same thing?"
teach.praise: Mean: add them up and divide by how many (25 ÷ 5 = 5). Median: arrange in order and take the middle one (also 5 here, but not always the same!).
teach.nudge: For the median, what do you do with the numbers before picking the middle one?

revise.summary: Mean = sum ÷ count; median is the middle value of ordered data; mode is the most frequent value. Outliers pull the mean but barely move the median.
focus: Find mean, median and mode.
Find the mean from a frequency table.
Choose the right average when there are outliers.
remember: Mean from a table = Σ(f × x) ÷ Σf.
Even count: median = mean of the two middle values.
traps: Arrange the data before finding the median.
Don't just average the values; use the frequencies.
The mean is not always the best average.

learn.hook: Section A averages 80 and Section B averages 60. Is the whole class average 70? Only if the sections are the same size!
points: Combined average = total of all values ÷ total count. It is NOT simply the mean of the group averages.
For two groups: n values with average a and m values with average b give combined average (na + mb)/(n + m). For three groups add a third term on top and a third count below.
Averaging the averages works only when the groups are the same size.

Uses: class sections of different sizes, rainfall over months of different lengths (weight by days), average price of shares bought in lots, and a cricket team's run rate over spells of different lengths.

example.q: Section A has 30 students averaging 80; Section B has 20 averaging 60. Find the combined average.

learn.reallife: A cricket team's overall run rate weights each spell by the number of overs, which is exactly a combined average.

games.title: Average traps
items: Two groups' averages can always be averaged to get the combined average.
Only when the groups are the same size.
The combined average lies between the two group averages.
It is a weighted mean of them.
If one group is larger, the combined average is closer to that group's average.
The larger group has more weight.
For three groups, add n₁a₁ + n₂a₂ + n₃a₃ and divide by n₁ + n₂ + n₃.
Same idea with one more group.
Monthly rainfall averages per day can be combined without caring about days in each month.
Weight each month by its number of days.

quiz.q: A class has 25 boys averaging 62 kg and 15 girls averaging 50 kg. What is the class average weight?
quiz.mistake: Takes the simple mean of 62 and 50

quiz.q: When is the combined average equal to the mean of the two group averages?
options: When the two groups are the same size
quiz.explain: With equal n, (na + nb)/(2n) = (a + b)/2.
steps: So it equals the mean of the averages only for equal-sized groups.
Answer: When the two groups are the same size
quiz.mistake: Thinks it is always true

quiz.q: Three sections have 20, 30 and 50 students with averages 70, 80 and 60. What is the overall average?
quiz.mistake: Averages 70, 80 and 60 equally

quiz.q: Ravi buys 40 shares at ₹120 and 60 shares at ₹95. What is his average price per share?
quiz.mistake: Takes the simple average of the two prices

quiz.q: A team scores at 7 runs per over for 10 overs and 4 runs per over for the next 40 overs. What is the run rate for the 50 overs?
quiz.explain: Runs = 70 + 160 = 230 in 50 overs.
quiz.mistake: Averages the two rates

quiz.q: February (28 days) had average daily rainfall 3 mm and March (31 days) had 5 mm. How should the average daily rainfall for both months be found?
quiz.explain: Weight each month's average by its number of days.
steps: The months have different numbers of days, so weight by days.
quiz.mistake: Ignores that the months have different lengths

quiz.q: The mean of 20 numbers is 15. A 21st number, 36, is added. What is the new mean?
quiz.explain: New total = 300 + 36 = 336, divided by 21.
quiz.mistake: Adds 36 to the mean

quiz.q: The combined average of groups with averages 40 and 70 is 60. Which group is larger?
quiz.explain: 60 is closer to 70, so that group has more weight.
steps: The simple mean of 40 and 70 is 55.
The combined average 60 is closer to 70.
So the group with average 70 has more weight (is larger).
quiz.mistake: Thinks the combined average is closer to the smaller group

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "Section A averages 80 and B averages 60. Is the whole class average 70?"
teach.praise: Wise! Find the total and divide by the total count; it's 70 only if the sections are the same size!
teach.nudge: What if one section has many more students? What should you find first?

revise.summary: A combined average is total of all values ÷ total count, not the mean of the group averages, unless the groups are the same size.
focus: Find combined averages of groups.
Find average prices and run rates.
Update a mean when a value is added.
traps: Don't average the averages for unequal groups.
Weight months by days.
The combined average is closer to the larger group's average.

learn.hook: Mix a weak sherbet and a strong one: the result is somewhere in between, but where?
points: Concentration of a mixture = total amount of the substance ÷ total quantity of mixture (often as a %).
Mixing two solutions: add up the substance in each and divide by the total volume. The result is a weighted average of the two strengths.
The result lies between the two strengths, closer to the strength of the larger quantity.
Dilution: adding x litres of water keeps the substance the same but increases the volume. Solve substance ÷ (old volume + x) = target.

example.q: Mix 2 L of 10% sugar syrup with 3 L of 20% syrup. Find the strength of the mixture.

learn.reallife: Making nimbu-pani or diluting a juice concentrate at home is exactly this kind of mixture problem.

items.q: 10 L of 25% salt: salt in L
6 L of 30% to make 20%: water to add (L)

games.title: Mixture sense
items: Mixing 10% and 20% solutions can give 25%.
The result must lie between 10% and 20%.
Adding water does not change the amount of sugar.
Only the volume increases.
Mixing more of the 20% solution makes the result closer to 20%.
It has more weight.
Concentration = substance ÷ total mixture.
That is the definition.
Adding water makes a solution stronger.
It becomes weaker (diluted).

quiz.q: A 5 L bucket of water has 0.4 L of dye. What is the concentration of dye?
quiz.mistake: Divides the wrong way

quiz.q: 4 L of 15% juice is mixed with 1 L of 40% juice. What is the strength of the mixture?
quiz.explain: Juice = 0.6 + 0.4 = 1 L in 5 L.
quiz.mistake: Takes the simple mean of 15% and 40%

quiz.q: 2 L of 30% acid is mixed with 6 L of 10% acid. The result is closer to:
options: 10%, because there is more of the 10% solution
quiz.explain: Result = (0.6 + 0.6)/8 = 15%, which is closer to 10%.
steps: There is more of the 10% solution, so it has more weight.
Answer: 10%, because there is more of the 10% solution
quiz.mistake: Thinks the stronger solution always dominates

quiz.q: What is the strength of the mixture in the previous question?
quiz.mistake: Adds the percentages

quiz.q: How much water must be added to 8 L of 25% syrup to make it 20%?
quiz.explain: Sugar = 2 L. 2 ÷ (8 + x) = 0.2 gives 8 + x = 10.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts percentages directly

quiz.q: Ananya has 3 L of 40% orange concentrate. She adds water to make a 15% drink. What is the final volume?
steps: Orange in the concentrate = 0.40 × 3 = 1.2 L (stays fixed).
quiz.mistake: Forgets that the orange amount stays fixed

quiz.q: A mixture has 30 L of milk and 10 L of water. What percentage is milk?
quiz.mistake: Divides milk by water

quiz.q: Equal volumes of 12% and 18% solutions are mixed. What is the strength?
quiz.explain: With equal volumes, the result is the simple average.
quiz.mistake: Adds the strengths

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "How do I find the strength of a mixture of two juices?"
teach.praise: Yes! Add the amounts of juice and divide by the total volume!
teach.nudge: What do you add up first? What do you divide by?

revise.summary: Concentration = substance ÷ total mixture. Mixing gives a weighted average strength between the two, closer to the larger quantity. Adding water keeps the substance fixed.
focus: Find concentrations.
Find the strength of a mixture.
Solve dilution problems.
remember: Equal volumes: simple average of strengths.
traps: Don't add or average percentages directly for unequal volumes.
The substance amount stays the same when diluting.
Divide by the total mixture, not by the water.

topics.title: Gold purity, mean depth and impossible targets

learn.hook: Melt a 22-karat ring and an 18-karat chain together. How pure is the new gold?
points: Gold purity is measured in karats (24 karat = pure) or, in old Indian texts, in varna (16 varna = pure).
Purity of combined gold = Σ(weight × purity) ÷ Σ weights, a weighted mean. Sridharacharya’s Patiganita (about 750 CE) has problems on melting together gold of different varna (16 varna = 24 karat).

Pits and pools dug to different depths appear in Brahmagupta’s Brahmasphutasiddhanta and in Prithudakasvami’s commentary on it (about 864 CE): the mean depth weights each section’s depth by its length, and volume = mean depth × length × width.
If the algebra gives a negative quantity (like −2 L of water), the target is impossible. You cannot reach 25% by mixing 10% and 20%, or make a solution stronger just by adding water.

example.q: 10 g of 22-karat gold is melted with 5 g of 16-karat gold. Find the purity of the alloy.

learn.reallife: Jewellers in India stamp gold with its karat; mixing old jewellery for remaking uses this weighted mean.

items.q: 10 g of 14 varna + 6 g of 16 varna: varna
Trench: 4 m at depth 2 m, 6 m at depth 3 m: mean depth (m)

games.title: Possible or impossible?
items: Mixing 10% and 20% acid can give 15%.
15% lies between them.
Mixing 10% and 20% acid can give 25%.
The result must lie between 10% and 20%.
Adding water to 30% syrup can make it 40%.
Water only dilutes.
Mixing 18k and 22k gold can give 20k.
It lies between 18 and 22.
If the equation says add −3 L of water, the target is impossible by adding water.
A negative quantity cannot be added.

quiz.q: 15 g of 20-karat gold is melted with 5 g of 24-karat gold. What is the purity of the alloy, in karats?
quiz.mistake: Averages 20 and 24 equally

quiz.q: In the varna system, how many varna is pure gold?
quiz.explain: Pure gold is 16 varna in old Indian texts (and 24 karat today).
steps: In old Indian texts, pure gold is 16 varna.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up varna with karat

quiz.q: 8 g of 12-varna gold and 8 g of 14-varna gold are melted together. What is the varna of the result?
quiz.explain: Equal weights, so the simple mean of 12 and 14.
quiz.mistake: Adds the varnas

quiz.q: A pit is 10 m long. The first 4 m are 3 m deep and the remaining 6 m are 2 m deep. What is its mean depth?
steps: Weight each depth by its length.
quiz.mistake: Takes the simple mean of 3 and 2

quiz.q: If the pit in the previous question is 2 m wide everywhere, what is its volume?
quiz.explain: Volume = mean depth × area = 2.4 × 10 × 2.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the width

quiz.q: Can you get a 30% salt solution by mixing 10% and 25% solutions?
options: No, the result must lie between 10% and 25%
quiz.explain: A mixture's strength is a weighted average, so it cannot exceed the stronger solution.
steps: A mixture's strength is a weighted average of 10% and 25%.
30% is outside, so it is impossible.
Answer: No, the result must lie between 10% and 25%
quiz.mistake: Thinks enough of the stronger solution can push past its own strength

quiz.q: Riya wants to turn 5 L of 20% juice into 25% juice by adding water. Solving 1 ÷ (5 + x) = 0.25 gives x = −1. What does this mean?
options: It is impossible by adding water; you would have to remove water
quiz.explain: A negative amount of water cannot be added.
steps: x = −1 means removing 1 L of water.
Adding water can only make it weaker.
Answer: It is impossible by adding water; you would have to remove water
quiz.mistake: Ignores the negative sign

quiz.q: Who among these described rules for mixing gold of different purities?
quiz.explain: Sridharacharya’s Patiganita (about 750 CE) includes problems on melting together gold of different varnas.
steps: Sridharacharya's Patiganita (about 750 CE) has problems on melting gold of different varna.
quiz.mistake: Picks a famous name without knowing the work

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "How do I find the purity when two pieces of gold are melted together?"
teach.praise: Shiny! Multiply each weight by its purity, add, and divide by the total weight!
teach.nudge: Does the heavier piece count more? How do you combine weights and purities?

revise.summary: Gold purity of an alloy is a weighted mean of purities. Mean depth weights each depth by its length. A negative answer in mixture problems means the target is impossible.
focus: Find the purity of melted gold.
Find mean depth and volume of pits.
Recognise impossible mixture targets.
remember: 10 g of 22 K + 5 g of 16 K → 20 K.
Sridharacharya (Patiganita, c. 750 CE); Brahmagupta and Prithudakasvami on pits.
traps: A mixture cannot be stronger than its strongest part.
Weight depths by length; don't average them simply.
A negative amount of water cannot be added.

learn.hook: Your final exam counts more than the class test? That's a weighted average with custom weights!
points: Weights can show importance, not just size: if Term 1, Term 2 and Final are weighted 3 : 2 : 5, the final counts most.
Weighted average = Σ(weight × score) ÷ Σ weights.
If tests have different maximum marks, first convert each to a percentage (marks ÷ maximum × 100), then apply the weights.
Star ratings: from a table of how many people gave 5★, 4★, ..., the average rating = Σ(stars × number) ÷ total people.
To design your own rating scheme (say for choosing a school trip), choose criteria, give each a weight that shows its importance, and compute the weighted score for each option.

example.q: Term 1: 70%, Term 2: 80%, Final: 90%, weighted 3 : 2 : 5. Find the overall score.

learn.reallife: Food-delivery apps show a restaurant's star rating as a weighted average of all customers' ratings.

games.title: Design a rating scheme
items: Choose the criteria (cost, distance, fun)
Give each criterion a weight
Score each option on each criterion
Multiply scores by weights and add
Divide by the total weight and compare

quiz.q: Marks 60, 75, 90 are weighted 1 : 1 : 2. What is the weighted average?
quiz.mistake: Takes the plain mean

quiz.q: A project is graded on idea (weight 2), work (weight 5) and presentation (weight 3). Kabir scores 8, 6 and 9. What is his weighted score?
quiz.mistake: Divides by 3 instead of the sum of weights

quiz.q: Riya gets 36/50 in Maths and 18/20 in a quiz. What are these as percentages?
quiz.mistake: Treats raw marks as percentages

quiz.q: Using those percentages with weights 3 : 1, what is Riya's overall percentage?
quiz.mistake: Weights raw marks instead of percentages

quiz.q: A product has ratings: 5★ by 12 people, 4★ by 6, 3★ by 2. What is the average rating?
quiz.mistake: Averages the star values without counting people

quiz.q: Why should marks out of different maximums be converted to percentages before weighting?
options: So that each mark is on the same scale
quiz.explain: 36/50 and 18/20 cannot be compared or combined until they are on a common scale.
steps: Marks out of 50 and out of 20 are on different scales.
Percentages put them on the same scale before weighting.
Answer: So that each mark is on the same scale
quiz.mistake: Adds raw marks with different maximums

quiz.q: A school weights homework 20%, tests 30% and the exam 50%. Meena gets 90, 70 and 60. What is her final score?
quiz.mistake: Takes the plain mean

quiz.q: A restaurant has 40 ratings of 5★ and 10 ratings of 1★. What is the average?
quiz.mistake: Averages 5 and 1

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "How do I find my final score when the exam counts more than the tests?"
teach.praise: Brilliant! Multiply each score by its weight, add, and divide by the total weight!
teach.nudge: How do you show that the exam matters more? What do you divide by at the end?

revise.summary: Weights can show importance. Weighted average = Σ(weight × score) ÷ Σ weights. Convert marks to percentages first when maximums differ.
focus: Compute weighted scores.
Convert marks to percentages before weighting.
Find average star ratings.
traps: Divide by the sum of weights, not the number of scores.
Don't weight raw marks with different maximums.
Count people when averaging star ratings.

topics.title: How weights behave, and overall profit

learn.hook: Double every weight and nothing changes! Add the same number to every weight and the scores start to look equal.
points: Multiplying all weights by the same number (like doubling them) leaves the weighted average unchanged: weights 1 : 3 and 2 : 6 give the same result.
Adding the same constant to every weight makes the weights more nearly equal, so the weighted mean moves towards the ordinary (simple) mean.
Overall profit % on several items = total profit ÷ total cost × 100. It is a weighted average of the individual profit rates, weighted by cost.

example.q: Scores 50 and 90 with weights 1 and 3. Find the weighted mean, then add 10 to each weight.
steps: Simple mean is 70; the new mean moved towards it

learn.reallife: A shopkeeper selling many items at different profit rates finds the shop's overall profit rate this way.

games.title: Weight rules
items: Doubling all weights doubles the weighted average.
It stays the same.
Weights 2 : 3 and 4 : 6 give the same weighted average.
One is just twice the other.
Adding a big constant to all weights brings the result close to the simple mean.
The weights become nearly equal.
Overall profit % is always the simple mean of the profit rates.
It must be weighted by cost.
If all weights are equal, the weighted mean equals the simple mean.
Equal weights treat all values alike.

quiz.q: Scores 60 and 100 have weights 3 and 1. What is the weighted mean?
quiz.mistake: Gives the simple mean

quiz.q: The weights in the previous question are changed to 6 and 2. What is the weighted mean now?
quiz.explain: Doubling all weights changes nothing: (360 + 200)/8 = 70.
steps: Doubling all weights leaves the average unchanged.
quiz.mistake: Doubles the average

quiz.q: Scores 60 and 100 with weights 3 and 1. If 100 is added to both weights (103 and 101), the weighted mean will be:
options: very close to 80, the simple mean
quiz.explain: Weights 103 and 101 are nearly equal, so the result ≈ (60 + 100)/2. (It is about 79.8.)
steps: That is very close to the simple mean (60 + 100) ÷ 2 = 80.
Answer: very close to 80, the simple mean
quiz.mistake: Thinks adding to weights has no effect

quiz.q: A shopkeeper buys pens for ₹800 and sells them at 15% profit, and notebooks for ₹1200 sold at 5% profit. What is his overall profit %?
quiz.explain: Profit = 120 + 60 = 180 on a cost of 2000.
steps: Profit on pens = 15% of 800 = 120; on notebooks = 5% of 1200 = 60.
quiz.mistake: Takes the simple mean of 15% and 5%

quiz.q: Item A costs ₹300 with 20% profit; item B costs ₹700 with 10% profit. Overall profit %?
quiz.mistake: Averages 20% and 10%

quiz.q: Why is overall profit % not the simple average of the rates?
options: Items with larger cost carry more weight
quiz.explain: The total profit depends on how much was spent on each item.
steps: Overall profit % = total profit ÷ total cost.
It is weighted by cost: items with larger cost count more.
Answer: Items with larger cost carry more weight
quiz.mistake: Ignores the size of each purchase

quiz.q: Weights 2 : 5 : 3 are scaled to 20 : 50 : 30. The weighted average:
quiz.explain: Multiplying every weight by 10 cancels out in Σwx ÷ Σw.
steps: Multiplying every w by 10 multiplies top and bottom by 10.
The 10s cancel, so the average stays the same.
quiz.mistake: Thinks larger weights give a larger answer

quiz.q: If every weight is the same, the weighted average equals:
quiz.explain: Equal weights treat every value alike.
steps: With equal weights w: Σwx ÷ Σw = wΣx ÷ (nw) = Σx ÷ n.
quiz.mistake: Confuses mean with median

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "If I double all the weights, does the weighted average change?"
teach.praise: Exactly! Doubling top and bottom cancels out, so it stays the same!
teach.nudge: What happens to Σwx and Σw when every weight doubles?

revise.summary: Multiplying all weights by the same number leaves a weighted average unchanged; adding the same constant to every weight moves it towards the simple mean. Overall profit % = total profit ÷ total cost.
focus: Predict how changing weights affects the average.
Find overall profit percentage.
Explain why it is a weighted average.
remember: Weights 1 : 3 and 2 : 6 give the same result.
traps: Don't take the simple mean of profit rates.
Scaling weights does not scale the answer.
Equal weights give the ordinary mean, not the median.

learn.hook: A picture is worth a thousand numbers! But a sneaky graph can also trick your eyes. Let's learn to read graphs like a detective.
points: Bar graphs show separate categories with bars of equal width and equal gaps between them.
A histogram shows grouped (continuous) data. The bars touch each other because the classes have no gaps.
If the classes in a histogram have unequal widths, adjust the heights so that the area of each bar is proportional to its frequency.
A frequency polygon is made by joining the mid-points (class marks) of the tops of the histogram bars with straight lines.
Line graphs show change over time. Always check the scale: an axis that does not start at 0 can make small differences look huge.

example.q: Classes 0–10, 10–20, 20–40 have frequencies 6, 9 and 12. What heights should the histogram bars have if a width of 10 is the standard?
steps: 0–10 and 10–20 have width 10, so heights stay 6 and 9
20–40 has width 20, twice the standard width

learn.reallife: Weather reports use line graphs for temperature, election coverage uses bar graphs, and doctors use histograms of patients' ages.

games.title: Pick the right graph
pairs: Temperature every hour of a day
Joining class marks of a histogram

games.title: Graph detective
items: In a histogram, there are no gaps between the bars
The classes are continuous, so each bar starts where the previous one ends.
In a bar graph the bars may have different widths
Bar graphs use equal widths so only the heights matter.
A frequency polygon joins the class marks of the bar tops
Each point is plotted at the middle of its class.
A graph whose vertical axis starts at 90 can make a small difference look big
Cutting off the bottom of the bars exaggerates the difference between them.
A line graph is the best way to show the favourite colours of a class
Favourite colours are separate categories, so a bar graph suits them better.

quiz.q: Why do the bars of a histogram touch each other?
options: To save space on the page
Because the classes are continuous with no gaps between them
Because it is a line graph
quiz.explain: In a histogram each class ends exactly where the next one begins, so the bars sit side by side.
steps: Histogram classes are continuous: each ends where the next begins.
So there are no gaps between the bars.
Answer: Because the classes are continuous with no gaps between them
quiz.mistake: Thinks a histogram is just a bar graph drawn closer together

quiz.q: In a frequency polygon, each frequency is plotted against which value of its class?
quiz.explain: The points of a frequency polygon are at the class marks, the middle of each class.
steps: A frequency polygon joins points at the middle of each class.
The middle of a class is its class mark.
quiz.mistake: Plots each point at the start of the class

quiz.q: Tickets sold at a school fair: Mon 20, Tue 35, Wed 15, Thu 40, Fri 30. What is the difference between the highest and lowest day's sales?
quiz.explain: Highest is Thursday (40) and lowest is Wednesday (15): 40 − 15 = 25.
quiz.mistake: Uses Monday as the lowest because it comes first

items: Mon
Tue
Wed
Thu
Fri

quiz.q: Monthly rainfall in a town: June 120 mm, July 300 mm, August 240 mm, September 150 mm. In which month was the rainfall exactly twice that of June?
quiz.explain: Twice June's rainfall is 2 × 120 = 240 mm, which is August.
quiz.mistake: Picks the tallest bar (July) without checking the numbers

items: Jun
Jul
Aug
Sep

quiz.q: Which graph is best for showing how the temperature changed hour by hour on a day?
options: A bar graph of favourite colours
quiz.explain: A line graph joins readings taken over time, making rises and falls easy to see.
steps: Temperature hour by hour is a change over time.
A line graph joins readings over time.
quiz.mistake: Chooses a histogram, which is for grouped data, not changes over time

quiz.q: A bar graph compares two shops' sales of 92 and 96 sweets, but its vertical axis starts at 90. Why does it look misleading?
options: The bars are the wrong colour
The axis does not start at 0, so a small difference looks very large
quiz.explain: Starting at 90, the bars look like 2 and 6 units tall, so one seems three times the other, though 96 is barely more than 92.
steps: With the axis starting at 90, bars look 2 and 6 units tall.
That makes 96 look three times 92, though they are close.
Answer: The axis does not start at 0, so a small difference looks very large
quiz.mistake: Reads only the heights of the bars without checking the scale

quiz.q: In a histogram, class 0–10 has frequency 5 and class 10–30 has frequency 20. Taking width 10 as standard, what should the adjusted height of the 10–30 bar be?
quiz.explain: The class 10–30 is twice the standard width, so its height is halved: 20 × 10 ÷ 20 = 10.
quiz.mistake: Uses the frequency as the height even though the class is wider

quiz.q: A bar graph shows Riya sold 45 laddoos and Meena sold 62 laddoos at the Diwali stall. How many more did Meena sell?
quiz.explain: Difference = 62 − 45 = 17 laddoos.
quiz.mistake: Adds the two bars instead of finding the difference

teach.ask: Gappu looks at two graphs: "Why are the bars in a histogram stuck together, but not in a bar graph?"
teach.praise: A histogram shows continuous classes, so its bars touch. A bar graph shows separate categories, so it has gaps. Got it!
teach.nudge: Is there any gap between the classes 10–20 and 20–30? What about between 'cricket' and 'football'?

revise.summary: Bar graphs show categories; histograms show grouped data with touching bars; frequency polygons join class marks; line graphs show change over time. Watch for misleading scales.
focus: Choose the right graph.
Read values and differences from graphs.
Adjust histogram heights for unequal classes.
remember: Histogram bars touch because classes are continuous.
Unequal class: adjusted height = frequency × standard width ÷ class width.
Frequency polygon points at class marks.
traps: An axis not starting at 0 can mislead.
Don't use raw frequency as height for a wider class.
A histogram is not just bars drawn closer.

learn.hook: One chart, three questions: which class won, what the total was, and what share each part had. Different charts answer different ones!
points: A clustered column chart puts bars for each group side by side within each category, so you can compare groups category by category.
A stacked bar chart piles the parts on top of each other: the full bar shows the total and each segment shows a part.
A 100% stacked bar chart makes every bar the same height (100%); each segment shows that part's share of its own total.

example.q: Class 9A: 18 girls, 12 boys. Class 9B: 15 girls, 25 boys. Describe the stacked and 100% stacked bars.
example.answer: Stacked bars show totals 30 and 40; 100% bars show shares 60/40 and 37.5/62.5

learn.reallife: News channels show election vote shares and cricket score breakdowns as stacked bars.

Show total sales and the part from each shop
Compare the share of each shop

quiz.q: Which chart best shows the total number of medals each state won and how many were gold, silver and bronze?
options: A pie chart of one state
quiz.explain: The full bar gives the total and the segments give each medal type.
steps: We need totals and parts for each state.
A stacked bar shows the total as the full bar and parts as segments.
quiz.mistake: Picks 100% bars, which hide the totals

quiz.q: Which chart is best for comparing, month by month, the rainfall in Chennai and Mumbai?
options: A frequency polygon of one city
quiz.explain: Bars for the two cities stand side by side in each month.
steps: We compare two cities in each month.
A clustered column chart puts their bars side by side per month.
quiz.mistake: Stacks two separate quantities that are not parts of one total

quiz.q: In a 100% stacked bar, what does the full height of every bar represent?
quiz.explain: Each bar is scaled to its own total, so all reach 100%.
steps: In a 100% stacked bar, each bar is scaled to its own total.
Answer: 100% of that bar's own total
quiz.mistake: Thinks bar heights show actual totals

quiz.q: A stacked bar for a school has segments: walk 120, bus 200, cycle 80. What is the total?
quiz.mistake: Reads only the largest segment

quiz.q: In that school, what percentage come by bus?
quiz.mistake: Uses the wrong total

quiz.q: In a 100% stacked chart, Village A's segment for 'farmers' is 70% and Village B's is 40%. What can you say?
options: A has more farmers than B
A larger share of A's workers are farmers
B has more workers than A
Both have the same number of farmers
quiz.explain: 100% bars show shares, not actual numbers.
steps: 100% bars show shares, not actual counts.
70% > 40%, so a larger share of A's workers are farmers.
We cannot tell which village has more farmers.
Answer: A larger share of A's workers are farmers
quiz.mistake: Reads shares as actual counts

quiz.q: A clustered chart shows a shop's sales of tea and coffee each day. On Monday the bars are 40 and 25. How many more cups of tea were sold?
quiz.mistake: Adds the bars

quiz.q: Class 8: 20 like cricket, 10 football. Class 9: 15 cricket, 15 football. In a 100% stacked chart, what is cricket's share in Class 8?
quiz.explain: 20 out of 30.
quiz.mistake: Uses the cricket count as a percentage

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "What's the difference between a stacked bar and a 100% stacked bar?"
teach.praise: Great! Stacked bars show totals and parts; 100% bars show each part's share!
teach.nudge: What does the full height of a stacked bar show? And of a 100% bar?

revise.summary: Clustered columns compare groups side by side; stacked bars show totals and parts; 100% stacked bars show each part's share of its own total.
focus: Choose clustered, stacked or 100% stacked charts.
Read totals and parts.
Find shares as percentages.
remember: Stacked bar total = sum of segments.
100% bars all reach the same height.
traps: 100% bars do not show actual numbers.
Don't stack quantities that are not parts of one total.
Use the right total when finding a share.

learn.hook: Two 100% bars look identical. Does that mean the two classes are the same size? Not at all!
points: Percentage of a part = part ÷ total × 100. Going back: part = percentage × total ÷ 100.
Equal 100% bars do not mean equal totals: 6 of 10 and 60 of 100 both show 60%.
From a stacked chart you can always make a 100% chart (you know the totals), but from a 100% chart alone you cannot get back the actual numbers.
Only draw conclusions the chart supports: a 100% chart tells you shares, not how many. A stacked chart tells you totals and parts, but not the reasons behind them.

example.q: In a 100% stacked chart, 35% of School P's students and 35% of School Q's students cycle to school. P has 400 students and Q has 1200. How many cycle in each?

learn.reallife: Advertisements often show '90% of users prefer...' without saying how many users were asked; always check the total.

games.title: Valid conclusion?
items: Equal 100% bars mean equal totals.
6/10 and 60/100 both give 60%.
A stacked chart can be turned into a 100% chart.
Divide each part by its bar's total.
A 100% chart alone gives the actual numbers.
The totals are missing.
If 40% of 50 is the part, the part is 20.
A bigger segment in a 100% chart always means a bigger actual count.

options: The actual number in each part
The share of each part in each bar
Which bar has the larger total

steps: A 100% chart shows only each part's share of its bar.
It does not show actual numbers, totals or reasons.
Answer: The share of each part in each bar

quiz.q: A stacked chart shows Shop X: tea 30, coffee 20; Shop Y: tea 45, coffee 30. In a 100% chart, how do the two bars compare?
options: They look the same: 60% tea and 40% coffee in both
steps: So the two 100% bars look the same.
Answer: They look the same: 60% tea and 40% coffee in both
quiz.mistake: Expects different shares because the totals differ

quiz.q: A survey shows 72 out of 120 students like maths. What percentage is this?
quiz.mistake: Uses the count as the percentage

quiz.q: 25% of a family's monthly spending of ₹36,000 is on food. How much is that?
quiz.mistake: Moves the decimal wrongly

options: The totals of the bars are not shown
quiz.explain: Part = % × total, and the total is unknown.
steps: Part = % × total, so the total is needed.
A 100% chart does not show the totals of the bars.
Answer: The totals of the bars are not shown

quiz.q: In a stacked chart, Team A's runs are 120 (fours) + 80 (others) and Team B's are 90 + 110. Which is a valid conclusion?

A will win the next match

It says nothing about sixes, skill or future matches.
Answer: A scored more runs in fours than B
quiz.mistake: Draws conclusions the chart cannot support

quiz.q: If 30% of the students is 54, how many students are there in all?
quiz.mistake: Multiplies instead of dividing

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "Two 100% bars look exactly the same. Do the classes have the same number of students?"
teach.praise: Correct! Same shares can come from very different totals!
teach.nudge: What does a 100% bar hide? Could 6 of 10 and 60 of 100 look the same?

revise.summary: Percentage of a part = part ÷ total × 100, and part = % × total ÷ 100. Equal shares can hide very different totals, so only draw conclusions the chart supports.

Find a total from a percentage.
Judge which conclusions a chart supports.
remember: A stacked chart can make a 100% chart, but not the other way round.

topics.title: Time-use charts and a better pie

learn.hook: Where do your 24 hours go? A 100% bar of your day might surprise you!
points: A time-use chart shows the share of a 24-hour day spent on each activity: 8 hours of sleep is 8/24 = 33⅓%. Smart watches show similar bars for body states like deep sleep, light sleep and active time.
Real data charts (species counts by group, wickets by type of bowler, objects orbiting the Earth by type) are read the same way: find the total, the parts and the shares.
A 100% stacked bar can replace a pie chart: both show parts of a whole.
Comparing shares across several 100% bars side by side is easier than comparing angles in several pie charts.
A family can track monthly spending (food, rent, travel, savings) as 100% bars, one per month, to see how shares change.

example.q: A student's day: sleep 8 h, school 7 h, study 3 h, play 2 h, other 4 h. Find each share.

learn.reallife: Fitness bands use stacked bars to show how your night's sleep splits into deep, light and REM sleep.

quiz.mistake: Thinks pies cannot show parts of a whole

quiz.mistake: Uses the amount instead of the share

steps: The amount grew, but the share is unchanged.

quiz.mistake: Uses the count itself instead of dividing by the total

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "How do I show how I spend my 24 hours as a chart?"
teach.praise: Lovely! Divide each activity's hours by 24 and draw a 100% bar!
teach.nudge: What is the total for a day? How do you turn hours into shares?

revise.summary: Time-use and real-data charts show shares of a whole, like hours of a 24-hour day. A set of 100% stacked bars is often clearer than several pie charts.

Read real-data charts.
Compare shares over time with 100% bars.
traps: Divide by 24 for a day, not 100.
A bigger amount is not always a bigger share.
Use the right total (e.g. 8 hours of sleep, not 24).

learn.hook: Your class has 40 marks scribbled on a page. In two minutes, can you say how many scored above 30? Organise the data and you can!
points: Data are facts or numbers collected for a purpose. Data you collect yourself are primary data; data taken from records or other sources are secondary data.
Raw data are data not yet arranged. Range = highest value − lowest value.
A frequency table shows how often each value (or group of values) occurs. Tally marks help you count.
For large data, use classes like 10–20, 20–30. Class width = upper limit − lower limit; class mark = (lower limit + upper limit) ÷ 2.
In classes such as 10–20 and 20–30, a value of exactly 20 is counted in 20–30 (the lower limit is included).

example.q: Marks of 12 students (out of 20): 12, 15, 8, 18, 15, 11, 9, 15, 17, 12, 6, 14. Make a frequency table with classes 5–10, 10–15, 15–20.

learn.reallife: The Census of India collects data from crores of households and organises it into tables so the government can plan schools, roads and hospitals.

quiz.q: What is the range of the data 12, 7, 19, 3, 15?
quiz.explain: Range = highest − lowest = 19 − 3 = 16.
quiz.mistake: Gives the highest value instead of the difference

quiz.q: What is the class mark of the class 20–30?
quiz.explain: Class mark = (20 + 30) ÷ 2 = 25, the middle of the class.
quiz.mistake: Gives the class width (10) or the sum of the limits (50)

quiz.q: What is the width of the class 45–60?
quiz.explain: Class width = upper limit − lower limit = 60 − 45 = 15.
steps: Class width = upper limit − lower limit.
quiz.mistake: Gives the class mark (52.5) instead of the width

quiz.q: Test scores of 10 students: 6, 8, 9, 5, 8, 10, 7, 8, 9, 4. How many students scored 8 or more?
quiz.explain: The scores 8 or more are 8, 9, 8, 10, 8 and 9: six students.
quiz.mistake: Counts only the scores above 8, leaving out the 8s

quiz.q: Classes are 0–10, 10–20, 20–30. In which class is a value of exactly 10 counted?
quiz.explain: In these classes the lower limit is included and the upper limit is not, so 10 goes into 10–20.
steps: The lower limit is included and the upper limit is not.
quiz.mistake: Counts a boundary value twice or in the lower class

quiz.q: Harpreet asks her classmates about their favourite festival and records the answers. What kind of data is this?
quiz.explain: She collected the data herself, first-hand, so it is primary data.
steps: Harpreet collected the answers herself, first-hand.
Data collected first-hand are primary data.
quiz.mistake: Thinks primary data must come from an official source

quiz.q: A frequency table for the number of siblings shows frequencies 5, 8, 12, 7 and 3. How many students were surveyed?
quiz.explain: The total number of students is the sum of the frequencies: 5 + 8 + 12 + 7 + 3 = 35.
steps: Students surveyed = sum of all frequencies.
quiz.mistake: Gives the largest frequency or the number of rows in the table

quiz.q: Kabir groups heights that are at least 140 cm and less than 170 cm into classes of width 5 cm (140–145, 145–150, ...). How many classes does he need?
quiz.explain: The heights cover 170 − 140 = 30 cm, and 30 ÷ 5 = 6 classes: 140–145 up to 165–170.
quiz.mistake: Counts the boundary points (7) instead of the gaps between them

teach.ask: Gappu has 50 numbers written in a messy list: "How can I make sense of all of them?"
teach.praise: Group the values into classes and count how many fall in each, using tally marks. A neat frequency table at last!
teach.nudge: What could you count to make the list easier to read? Could you put the values into groups?

revise.summary: Data can be primary (collected yourself) or secondary. Organise raw data with frequency tables and classes; range = highest − lowest.
focus: Find range, class width and class mark.
Make frequency tables with tallies and classes.
Place boundary values correctly.
remember: Class width = upper − lower; class mark = (lower + upper) ÷ 2.
In 10–20, 20–30, a value of 20 goes in 20–30.
traps: Don't confuse class width with class mark.
Count a boundary value only once, in the upper class.
Total surveyed = sum of frequencies, not the largest one.
